Background
Introductory Concepts and Terminology

COVID-19 Pandemic
• The COVID-19 Pandemic led to, arguably, the largest educational disruption in
 the history of the United States.
• Two-and-a-half years into the pandemic and the impacts of the pandemic are
 still being felt.
• The pandemic impacted students academically, emotionally, physically, and
 financially.
• In this overview, we address three things:
 • Academic Impact: What is it and what happened to students in Hawaii?
 • Academic Recovery: What is it and what is happening to students in Hawaii
 currently?
 • Now What?: How can impact and recovery data be leveraged to help
 students going forward? Evidence-based investigations of what is working.

What is Academic Impact?
• The pandemic and all the ensuing disruptions functioned/
 functions as an “academic headwind”, impeding (in general)
 the academic progress of students.
• Headwinds impede progress in two ways:
 ▪ They slow one’s rate of progress (speedometer)
 ▪ And by slowing one’s rate of progress they lead to less distance being travelled
 (odometer).
• In education these two impediments manifest as:
 ▪ Decrease in student growth (i.e. decrease in velocity = deceleration).
 ▪ Decrease in student attainment.

 4

Assessment Data
• We investigated the impacts in achievement and growth of the pandemic
 across two time frames:
 • Impact: Spring 2020 through Summer 2021
 • Recovery: Fall 2021 through Summer 2022
• To investigate impact we utilized two primary sources of data
 • State summative assessment data (SBA)
 • Impact: SBA Spring 2019 to Spring 2021 (SBA testing cancelled in 2020)
 • Recovery: SBA Spring 2021 to Spring 2022
 • State English Language Proficiency Data (ACCESS)
 • Impact: ACCESS Winter 2020 to Winter 2021
 • Recovery: ACCESS Winter 2021 to Winter 2022

Recovery Phase
• During the 2021-2022 academic year, school returned to normal for most
 students.
• The hope was that a return to normal would lead recovery of the academic losses
 incurred by students.
• Because learning slowed during the initial phase of the pandemic, to make up for
 those losses, learning must accelerate to rates above normal in order to catch-up
 for those loses.
• Data from two sources was utilized to examine whether recovery is occurring:
 • SBA data from 2021 and 2022
 • WIDA-ACCESS data from 2021 and 2022

Overall Recovery
• Analysis of 2022 SBA and ACCESS data indicates a lot of trends in Hawaii to be
 happy about.
• In both ELA and mathematics, learning acceleration was at least as much to be
 considered stabilization and in many cases could be considered as genuine
 recovery.
• Compared to a dozen other states that the Center conducts these analyses, Hawaii
 comes out as the best in terms of pandemic recovery.
• Results from 2023 data will be critical to assess whether these exemplary rates of
 learning (beyond what the state experience pre-COVID) are being maintained.

Now What
Leveraging Assessment Data to Help Students Overcome COVID-19 Academic Impacts

Exemplar Schools: Impact & Recovery
• Original discussions about examining ROI were redirected to examine Return on Activities:
 • Identify outlier schools in terms of impact/recovery.
 • Investigate whether activities (or lack thereof) could potentially be responsible for the
 school’s outlier status.
 • For schools with plausible activities leading to exemplary recovery, investigate links to
 relevant investment/funding.
• Step 1 is to find these outlier schools.
• We investigated schools along two dimensions:
 • Academic Impact (2019 to 2021 decrease in student learning)
 • Academic Recovery (2021 to 2022 increase in student learning relative to pre-
 pandemic 2018-2019 learning)
